plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a slice of the plenoptic function sampled at four spatial locations: two in free space and two inside a pinhole camera. At each location, the plenoptic function encodes the intensity of light rays passing through that point from every direction. The locations inside the pinhole camera show that most directional values are zero, with only specific directions carrying non-zero intensity due to the camera aperture. The figure introduces the plenoptic function as a complete representation of all light in a scene, motivating its use in neural radiance fields (NeRFs).

interactionPlan.concept: The plenoptic function assigns every point in space an angular distribution of incoming light, which is dense in open space but sparse inside a pinhole camera because the aperture admits only a few ray directions.

stylized tree on the right with green leafy canopy and brown trunk as the visible scene object
pinhole camera on the left drawn as a black rectangular box with a small aperture opening on the right side
large text label 'Pinhole camera' above the camera
two red sampling points inside the camera near the image plane
two red sampling points in free space between the camera and the tree
black ray lines with arrowheads converging toward each red sampling point
dense radial ray bundle around each free-space sampling point showing many incoming directions
sparse ray bundle inside the pinhole camera showing only directions that pass through the aperture
crossing ray paths from the tree through the pinhole to the camera interior
angular light distribution glyph centered on the currently selected sampling point
highlight ring around the currently selected sampling point
annotation showing 'many nonzero directions' for free-space samples
annotation showing 'mostly zero directions' for inside-camera samples

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A NeRF-like scene representation is powerful because it can be viewed as learning this position-and-direction dependent light field: light at every point, from every direction.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a wide left-to-right layout: pinhole camera on the left, two free-space samples in the center, and a stylized tree on the right. Draw red circular sampling points and black incoming ray arrows. In free-space mode, show a dense starburst of rays around the selected point; in inside-camera mode, dim or omit most directions and leave only a few rays passing through the camera aperture. Keep the tree bright green with a brown trunk, the camera outline black, and the sampling points saturated red so the contrast between scene, geometry, and sampled plenoptic values is immediately clear.

authoredContext:
Given a scene, the plenoptic function is a full description of all the
light rays that travel across the space (-nerfs-plenoptic_function).
The plenoptic function tells us the light intensity of a light ray
passing through the three-dimensional (3D) point $(X, Y, Z)$ from the
direction given by the angles $(\psi, \phi)$, with wavelength $\lambda$,
at time $t$: $$L(X, Y, Z, \psi, \phi, \lambda, t)$$ In this chapter wewill ignore time and we will only use three color channels instead of
the continuous wavelength. We can represent the plenoptic function with
the parametric form $L_{\theta}$ where the parameters $\theta$ have to
be adapted to represent each scene.

Plenoptic function . The figure shows a slice of the plenoptic function at four locations. Two of the locations are in free space, and two other locations are inside a pinhole camera.

An image gets formed by summing all the light rays that reach each
sensor on the camera (that is, we sum over a section of the plenoptic
function). -nerfs-plenoptic_function shows an illustration of the
plenoptic function at four points, two of them are inside a pinhole
camera and are used to form an image of what is outside. The plenoptic
function inside the pinhole camera has most of the values set to zero
and only specific directions at each location have non-zero values.

discrepancies: The overall composition is heavily compressed: the camera, ray bundles, and tree are much smaller and closer together than in the source, where the camera occupies the left lower area, the ray fields are large and central, and the tree dominates the right side.

The generated default view adds yellow selection rings, dashed circular angular glyphs, tick marks, and explanatory annotations around the free-space red point; these overlays are not present in the source and visually change the clean red-dot/ray depiction.

The tree is much smaller and more cartoon-like than the source tree, with a simplified canopy and trunk instead of the large irregular green canopy and tall brown trunk occupying the right third of the figure.

The pinhole-camera ray geometry is not as clean as the source: the source shows two clear ray crossings through the pinhole from the right-side samples to the two red points in the camera, while the generated version has extra/duplicated thin ray bundles and sparse direction arrows near the camera points.
The two free-space ray stars are smaller and partly cluttered by the added glyphs and labels, whereas the source shows large unobstructed radial arrow fields around the two red points.
A large instructional UI panel occupies substantial space in the rendered default state, so the figure does not read as a drop-in replacement for the static textbook image.
evaluation.notes: The main components of the pinhole-camera scene are present and the interactions are meaningful, but the default visual is cluttered with added explanatory overlays and has substantially different proportions from the source.

Simplify the camera ray paths to the two clean pinhole-crossing ray bundles shown in the source, avoiding extra sparse direction bundles around the camera red points in the default view.
Increase and reposition the 'Pinhole camera' label to better match the source hierarchy, and remove or enlarge tiny added labels that are not readable at inline size.
